newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World telecoms trade booming in digital age - survey.
newsitem.headline: World telecoms trade booming in digital age - survey.

text.p: World trade in telecommunications is booming with global revenues forecast to jump to more than $1.2 trillion by 2000 and the market will expand further in the coming digital age, a U.N. survey said on Friday.

Consumers are making more international calls, privatisation is luring foreign investors to the industry, interest in mobile communications and new services is rising and demand is fuelling a boom in new computer networks like the Internet, it said.

The survey by the International Telecommunications Union, the specialised U.N. telecoms agency, was issued as talks moved towards a finale in Geneva to hammer out a global pact to free up the market, inject competition and slash the cost of telephone calls for ordinary people and for businesses.

The United States, the world's largest single telecoms market, holds the key to the success of the talks and is still pressing hard for further improvements a day before Saturday's deadline for an accord, trade diplomats said.

The ITU survey predicted total world revenues from the industry could almost double by 2000 from $800 billion in 1996 if a deal is struck, boosting information technology industries and cutting the cost of communications networks.
"The global trend now is towards a freeing up of markets and this is expected to lead to strong growth in international trade in services," it said.

The ITU survey said total sales in telecommunications stood at nearly $800 billion -- three-quarters of which came from services -- and the industry now ranked third in the world in terms of market capitalisation behind health care and banking.
The telecommunications sector is growing at twice the rate of the global economy at an average annual rate of seven percent.

Convergence with information, broadcasting and communication technology industries -- worth some $1.37 trillion in 1995 -- is fuelling more growth in the industry, thanks to the growing number of users of electronic on-line systems, it said.
The survey put the value of transactions carried out via the Internet global computer system by around 50 million users at up to $3 billion in 1996.

It said telecoms privatisation around the world was luring foreign investment, particularly in mobile communications, and countries failing to open up their domestic markets to outside competition would risk losing foreign investors.
"The new paradigm for international trade in telecommunications is based on global competition," it said. "The telecommunications environment is changing from a world of one-to-one relations."

Exports of telecoms equipment rose by 20 percent to around $60 billion in 1995, while international telephone calls are growing at a rate of 15 percent a year, generating $53 billion in retail revenues worldwide in 1995 or nearly 10 percent of total retail revenues.
